title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
description: At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.The region's G
body: At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five.A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit.Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week.Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing.It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July.Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday.St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible.Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning.Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire. It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes".As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions.Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections.Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism, including from some US Republicans.However, on Sunday, Zelensky said on Telegram he had had conversations with Trump's top negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.He said their teams are in constant communication and preparing the next diplomatic steps.Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year.Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter.Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.

schema.headline: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg

title: Champions Cup: Northampton Saints 28-12 Cardiff - Prem club wins Champions Cup opener
description: Investec Champions CupNorthampton (14) 28Tries: Pater, Thame, Hendy, Dingwall Cons: Belleau 3, PaterCardiff (0) 12Tries: Millard, Grady Con: EvansNort
body: Investec Champions CupNorthampton (14) 28Tries: Pater, Thame, Hendy, Dingwall Cons: Belleau 3, PaterCardiff (0) 12Tries: Millard, Grady Con: EvansNorthampton became the only English side to win in the opening round of the Champions Cup by battling past Cardiff.Saints, quarter-finalists last season, scored four tries at Franklin's Gardens in a nervy Pool Four encounter.The English champions led 14-0 at half-time thanks to efforts in tricky conditions by James Pater and Toby Thame.Tenacious Cardiff struck back through Harri Millard and Mason Grady to make it a two-point game in the final quarter.But George Hendy and Fraser Dingwall responded as Northampton got off to a winning start, albeit without a bonus point.Northampton's success came at the end of a chastening opening weekend of the top-tier tournament for Prem clubs, with Gloucester drawing against champions Bordeaux-Begles but six other sides losing.Cardiff's return to the top tier of Europe after two seasons in the Challenge Cup was a considerable one.Saints had scored 24 tries in their three opening fixtures of their Prem title defence, including 11 against Bath last time out at Franklin's Gardens.The Welsh side also had to contend with a five-day turnaround to a United Rugby Championship (URC) fixture against Sharks at Cardiff Arms Park.That led to several influential players being held back, although they did give first appearances of the season to Wales and Lions internationals Taulupe Faletau and Josh Adams after injury.Northampton also made changes because of a big fixture on the horizon - the short trip to Leicester on Saturday - but got the job done.Full-back Pater opened the scoring for Saints with a supporting run and centre Thame crashed over after 20 minutes.Both Northampton number eight Callum Chick and Cardiff lock Tom Manz knocked on going for the line as slippery conditions led to it being 14-0 at half-time.The Blue and Blacks struck back early in the second half when centre Millard hit a nice line in the 22 and then defended stoutly to frustrate their hosts, forcing them into a raft of handling errors.It was 14-12 on the hour when, after Saints fly-half Anthony Belleau was sin-binned for a breakdown offence, the ball was floated to the right by Jarrod Evans for Grady to cross.Cardiff scented an upset only for Hendy to respond swiftly, juggling the ball for a try that Pater converted.The Northampton wing went from scoring five points to saving them by chasing down Adams when a try seemed certain.Dingwall dashed over in the 78th minute but the hosts could not find the fifth try that was needed for a five-point haul.Northampton: Pater; Sleightholme, Hutchinson, Thame, Hendy; Belleau, Mitchell; Fischetti, Smith, Kundiona, Lockett, van der Mescht, Kemeny, Taylor, Chick.Replacements: Langdon, Els, Neculai, Prowse, Ulcoq, McParland, Smith, Dingwall.Yellow card: Belleau 60.Cardiff: Young; Grady, Millard, Emanuel, Bowen; Evans, Mulder; Southworth, D Hughes (capt), Wainwright, Manz, Thornton, Paea, D Thomas, Faletau.Replacements: E Lloyd, Barratt, Cowell, McNally, De La Rua, S Davies, Sheedy, Adams.Referee: Jeremy Rozier (France)Assistant referees: Thomas Charabas (France) & Cyrille Boulay (France)TMO: Julien Castaignede (France)

schema.headline: Champions Cup: Northampton Saints 28-12 Cardiff - Prem club wins Champions Cup opener

title: Cindy Crawford 'beyond heartbroken' after death of son Presley at 27
description: Supermodel Cindy Crawford has said she and her family are "beyond heartbroken" over the death of her son Presley Gerber."He is a sweet, beautiful soul
body: Supermodel Cindy Crawford has said she and her family are "beyond heartbroken" over the death of her son Presley Gerber."He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever," she posted on Instagram, next to a black-and-white photo of him. "We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability."The 27-year-old died on 20 September at a rehab facility in California. Police said officials are investigating his death as a suspected overdose.Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his catwalk debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.Crawford wrote in the post on Sunday: "We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years.""We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain," she also posted."Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia," she wrote in closing, with an emoji of angel wings.The tribute also listed the dates of his birth and death. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner lists Gerber's case as pending additional investigation. The Santa Monica Police Department has said there is no indication foul play was involved in his death.Gerber's sister Kaia also dedicated a post to him on Sunday which included a video of the two siblings as children dancing together, a photo of them standing near the ocean, and a four-page letter to "prez" typed out on a blue background.In the letter, she said she had been scared of getting her ears pierced, so "you went first"."But when I held the earring they took from your body, all I could think was: That belongs to you," she wrote. "I am learning how to love you when I cannot see you," she also wrote. "How to tell you something without picking up my phone to call you. How to be your sister in a world that I can't reach for you in," she wrote. In recent years, Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use and frequently posted videos on Instagram himself for what he called "Mental Health Mondays".His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.If you're affected by any of the issues in this article you can find details of organisations who can help via the BBC Action Line.Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external, external.

schema.headline: Cindy Crawford 'beyond heartbroken' after death of son Presley at 27

title: Green Party leader Zack Polanski says he will not overturn Zionism motion
description: Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.The Green leader told Sunday
body: Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.The Green leader told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, it would be party policy until 2028.The motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month, described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".It divided the party and sparked a major backlash from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and the European Green movement, with the equality watchdog writing to the party for more information on it.The fallout from the motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which he came second to Labour, and threatened his leadership.He came under criticism for not voting on the motion which was passed by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the party's 230,000 members - in Brighton earlier this month.The motion also asserted the party's backing for "a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine", a full arms embargo on Israel and a commitment to Palestinian liberation. Asked if he would now step in as leader to overturn it, Polanski said: "I'm not going to try to overturn it."At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it - I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves."He said this would not be until 2028 as "you can't [amend it] within the rules, so when you vote on something in our party conference that's then policy for two years".Kuenssberg asked if he would therefore change the rules as leader, but Polanski said: "I think if members have made a decision, then I respect the democratic will of our members."Former Green Party co-leader and current MP Adrian Ramsay responded by calling for action to be taken sooner. "I don't think it's tenable for us to continue the next two years with this policy that's been adopted given the huge political distraction that it's been for our councillors across the country," he told the BBC News Channel. "One way forward could be to have a ballot of all party members to establish very clearly where does the party as a whole stand - my view is we would see a different answer."Polanski had previously said he would not have voted for the motion without two amendments.The first of these would have avoided "determining there was a single democratic state", and the other would have specified that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish Green members who attend synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.Both of these amendments were voted down by members at the party's conference.Green MPs, including Ellie Chowns, have called for the party's member-led decision-making procedures to be reviewed given how few people took part in the vote.Asked if he thought Zionism was racist, Polanski said he did not think this was controversial, adding: "I think what's controversial is that 75,000 Palestinians have been murdered in the last few years."Kuenssberg asked Polanski if he accepted that for many Jewish people, Zionism was the right to have a safe place to live, or homeland."I think that's what people think it means, but actually in practical application - which is what we're talking about here - that homeland has come to the cost of the Palestinian people," Polanski, who is Jewish, said."I want equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - the practical application of Zionism has not resulted in that."When questioned if he thought Israel had a right to exist, he said he did not think "any state has a right to exist under international law".And asked if he would apologise for his handling of the row, as the Jewish Greens chair Vivien Lichtenstein has asked him to do, Polanski said: "I'm not sorry at all."In response, Phil Rosenberg, president of the Board of Deputies of British Jews, accused Polanski of being "all over the place" on the issue."Let us remember that, as of now, the Green Party's platform erases Jewish identity and experience, calls for Israel's elimination, and tells the vast majority of Jews, who overwhelmingly believe in the right of Israel to exist, that they are not welcome in the party," Rosenberg added.Polanski has said no Jewish Green members will be excluded based on their faith or background - and that being Jewish and supporting Israel are "two separate things".His latest comments come after a fortnight of criticism from across the political spectrum over the motion.Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disown the motion while Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it "antisemitic". Polanski said it was up to Green councillors to do what they saw fit.

schema.headline: Green Party leader Zack Polanski says he will not overturn Zionism motion

title: Madueke shows level of 'anger and conviction' to prove he is more than a finisher
description: Noni Madueke may not have the starting role he wants at Arsenal, but his winning goal against Nottingham Forest showed why he is one of Mikel Arteta's
body: Noni Madueke may not have the starting role he wants at Arsenal, but his winning goal against Nottingham Forest showed why he is one of Mikel Arteta's valued "finishers".The England international scored in the second half to earn Arsenal a 1-0 result and three valuable points towards their defence of the Premier League title.Madueke has started just one top-flight game this season, the 2-1 win over Leeds that came eight days prior to their victory over Oliver Glasner's Forest on Sunday.Arsenal's summer was dominated by talk of their search for an elite forward, with the left wing one of the positions identified.But after unsuccessful pursuits of superstar players such as Vinicius Jr and Julian Alvarez, the only new addition in that position was Christos Tzolis, the winger brought in to replace the outgoing Leandro Trossard.Tzolis has started the season well and has been the first-choice winger for Arteta, meaning that Madueke and Eberechi Eze have had to be content with the majority of their minutes coming from the bench or in the Carabao Cup.However, Tzolis is now out with a hamstring injury picked up while playing for Greece, and that has presented a chance for Madueke to show Arteta why he should be considering the former Chelsea man as much more than a finisher - the term Arteta uses for his substitutes.Madueke did well when starting against Leeds, praised by Arteta for being the best player at the club during the international break. The Arsenal boss said the winger "grabbed it [his start] with both hands".The England international also started on the right wing, his more natural position, against Lille in a Champions League win on Tuesday, assisting the opening goal.Against Forest on Sunday, Madueke was introduced at half-time by Arteta and said he took the manager's instructions with him on to the pitch."Hang in there, stick to the gameplan, go out there and try to attack the opposition, be dangerous, be yourself and be good defensively as well," Madueke said.He scored with a deflected shot in the 80th minute when he took on defender Daniel Munoz and cut in on his weaker right foot."I'd beaten him on the outside a couple of times so I thought I'll come inside and just let rip," Madueke said.It's fair to say that the Arsenal fans have not always taken to Madueke since his move from London rivals Chelsea.There was a 'No to Madueke' petition started when he joined the club and his performances have been criticised for being inconsistent.But since his £48.5m arrival, Madueke has helped the club lift their first Premier League title in 22 years and played a big part as Arsenal reached the Champions League final.Madueke scored eight goals and provided four assists in 43 appearances in all competitions last season, but questions over his end product remain.He is one of Arsenal's most direct players, and England manager Thomas Tuchel and his staff also rate the winger as one of the best players in one-versus-one situations."Noni, look at me, a smile on my face because he is a special character," Arteta said when he was asked about Madueke's character."It's someone that's very much loved in and around the dressing room. The way he connects, talks with people. He is just a special guy."I think I saw an interview where they were asking a few of our players 'who would you call if you had a problem?' And some of them said Noni, which I was surprised."But I think it is a massive credit and describes the type of person he is."The 24-year-old has now put in three good performances in a row."He is in a good moment," Arteta said. "After the break, he is showing something else, another level of anger, another level of conviction as well as in his actions and he is becoming decisive in matches, which is what we expect from a player like him."He is a player that doesn't really mind left or right, but he has played many more minutes on the right side. The team needs him there at the moment and he is doing well."Arteta has made a big point of referring to his substitutes as "finishers" as he points to the importance of the squad.That mentality is seeming to have the desired effect. Since the start of last season, Arsenal substitutes have contributed to 26 Premier League goals, which is more than any other side in the league.Bruno Guimaraes scored the winner against Leeds after coming off the bench last time out in the league, while substitutes Bukayo Saka, Kai Havertz and captain Martin Odegaard played a major role in the last two goals in the win over Lille.But Arteta is not concerned the Gunners are overly reliant on players from the bench."There have been other games as well that we have had to score in the first half," Arteta said."We have played 11 competitive matches and we won 10. We are getting a variety of ways to win in many different contexts."Arteta said he expected few chances against a well organised Forest at the City Ground but added: "I had the belief that the moment the physical level was going to drop, the spaces would be a little bit bigger, the timing more and we would be more efficient there."And the finishers delivered because the context of the game changed a little bit."

schema.headline: Madueke shows level of 'anger and conviction' to prove he is more than a finisher

title: How The Traitors' music plays with your emotions
description: Making murder fun: How the Traitors' soundtrack sets the toneFigure caption, Watch: How does music on The Traitors manipulate your emotions?ByMusic co
body: Making murder fun: How the Traitors' soundtrack sets the toneFigure caption, Watch: How does music on The Traitors manipulate your emotions?ByMusic correspondentSuspicion, intrigue, treachery, Claudia Winkleman. The Traitors has it all.But the shadowiest of the show's shadowy secrets is its music.Have you ever noticed how the soundtrack manipulates your perception? A sinister orchestral flourish hints at a double cross. A cheeky chord injects humour into a kitchen conflab.As ever, though, you shouldn't trust what happens in the castle. The music can provide emphasis or act as misdirection, all at the producers' behest.Duplicity was baked into the music from the beginning."I remember the BBC was quite reluctant to even think about a show with murder as a main feature, so I knew I didn't want the music to go really dark," says Sam Watts, who composed the opening theme and much of the incidental score (but is not responsible for the show's haunting cover versions of well-known pop songs... more on those later).Watts, who had previously worked on Planet Earth and The Sarah Jane Adventures, pitched to work on the programme with only a basic idea of the set-up. It was only when he learned Winkleman was the host that he settled on his approach."They sent me a little shot they'd done of the opening with Claudia and the castle. That's when I knew it was going to be a bit camp and high drama and all the glorious things that Claudia brings to the show. So I just went with that - dark but fun."Image source, Sam WattsImage caption, Sam Watts' Traitors theme helped to establish the show's identityFor the title sequence, the 44-year-old wanted something memorable. As a kid, his favourite song was Bernard Hoffer's gloriously over-the-top Thundercats theme, external, so that's the level he aspired to."I was trying to write something that signified the show was starting, so that people would run in from making their cup of tea in the kitchen to watch it."And I wanted a memorable melody that people could hum, because it helps with the identity of the show."The Traitors theme is "one of the biggest pieces of music I've ever written", he says, recorded with a full orchestra and overdubbed with dozens of electronic elements to create a heightened, hyperreal atmosphere.That bled into the 20 or so other pieces Watts wrote, which also appear in dozens of international spin-offs.The idea, he says, is that the whole hour feels like a film trailer, with viewers permanently waiting for the psychological pressure chamber to explode.To achieve that, he employed several techniques of trailer music - most notably the "Braam", a klaxon-like punctuation mark invented for Christopher Nolan's Inception (see video for a fuller exploration).Show producer Sarah Fay took that concept and amplified it. "We wanted to just supersize it and make it feel like a drama, not like your usual reality [show]," she said in a rare interview with Metro, external when the first civilian series aired in 2022."We wanted to make it feel like that edge-of-your-seat cinematic drama with, you know, elements of Succession, and we wanted it to feel like Knives Out when you get into the castle!"To achieve that, she commissioned additional music from film trailer composers, including Hans Zimmer's company Bleeding Fingers. But she also sprinkled in a handful of creepy cover versions.Some became instant classics - such as a sinister spin on Britney Spears' Toxic, external, or a version of Tears For Fears' Mad World, external seemingly broadcast on a tannoy from Hades.They're so integral to The Traitors' aesthetic that it might surprise you to learn they weren't recorded specifically for the show.Image caption, The Traitors score has proved so popular that an entire BBC Proms concert was devoted to the show's music last yearBoth examples were created by German writer-producers 2wei.Based in Hamburg, they had no idea their music had appeared in The Traitors until friends in the UK messaged them in excitement."We were just flipping out," says 2wei's Simon Heeger. "It's completely different to how we ever thought it would be used."Heeger founded 2wei, pronounced "zwei", in 2016 with his old college friend Christian Vorländer.They had both spent time in LA working on advertisements and (stop me if you're sensing a theme here) film trailers, before moving home to build a music production empire."Christian worked on the Mad Max soundtrack, which is really known for the big drums and the orchestral scale – and that was really the starting point of our sound," says Heeger."Whenever you hear big epic drums with an orchestral sound and maybe a female vocal on top of it, it's usually something we had our fingers in."Image source, 2weiImage caption, Simon Heeger is the co-founder of 2wei, which is responsible for some of Traitors' most memorable cover songsTheir big break came with a stormy reworking of Destiny's Child's Survivor, which featured in the trailer to Alicia Vikander's Tomb Raider, external.Since then, their music has appeared in films like Wonder Woman and video games such as League of Legends. In The Traitors, original 2wei songs like Blindside, external now feature alongside their covers (other producers, including SYML and Damned Anthem also contribute songs to the show).Heeger says their background in commercials makes the music perfectly suited to the show's slippery skullduggery."In adverts, you only have a few seconds to convey a certain emotion and, especially in Traitors, where there are cliffhangers and moments that you don't expect, you need music that comes to the point right away but still has a boldness to it."It's a sweet spot, and it's not easy to convey, but every now and then it works quite well."Fans agree. On Spotify, there are hundreds of playlists dedicated to the programme's background music. Some are tailored to murder mystery parties and Halloween events. Others compile more sedate moments under labels like "gentle tension" or "chill elder emo watching Traitors".But never forget: the soundtrack is playing a deceitful game of its own."A lot of my music has a wink in it and, for The Traitors, it's a little silly and slightly over the top," says Watts."I think it helps the nastier side of things - the murder, the plotting - feel a bit more fun."

schema.headline: How The Traitors' music plays with your emotions

title: Canadian military base fire: Death toll confirmed and cause under investigation
description: What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military baseImage source, ReutersImage caption, The busy training base is located behind fences on
body: What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military baseImage source, ReutersImage caption, The busy training base is located behind fences on remote land in AlbertaByJack BurgessUpdated 29 minutes agoA huge fire swept through a Canadian military base on Saturday, killing at least four people and leaving 19 people in critical condition.Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as one of the worst peace time tragedies on Canadian soil in the history of the military. Here is what we know about the deadly incident so far.How did the fire start?The fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright broke out at around 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT).Major-General Wade Rutland, Commander of 1st Canadian Division, said a grass fire ignited on a training range and "uncommonly strong winds caused it to spread rapidly and shift direction" towards soldiers taking part in exercises. He said the cause of the initial fire remains under investigation. Earlier, local media reported it may have been started when a gas main was struck during a live firing exercise, but the military later said that investigators do not believe any explosions were caused by oil or gas infrastructure.Carney described the fire as "violent" and "fast-moving".The prime minister said military and civilian fire crews "fought this fire throughout the night in some of the worst conditions imaginable, risking their lives to protect their fellow Canadians".The Canadian defence ministry has said the cause remains under investigation, and "at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".Figure caption, Carney: 'Canada must now serve' service members killed in fireHow many people have been killed?Four service members are confirmed to have died, while a further 39 people are in hospital - 19 of whom are in critical condition.Officials have not indicated whether or not the government expects the death toll to rise but said many people had suffered severe burns.On Saturday evening, Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton declared a code orange - a disaster response protocol for a high-casualty incident. It was stood down on Sunday afternoon.Alberta's health service said the emergency response lasted for 10 hours, and involved 22 ambulances and eight aircraft. Ongoing care for the injured is expected to be "intensive", a statement continued. A stream of ambulances were seen arriving at the hospital and one doctor told Canadian public broadcaster CBC that the facility had been "completely overwhelmed" by the number of patients. Where is the base?Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is located in a rural area of the western province of Alberta - around 120 miles (193km) from Edmonton and 180 miles (290km) from Calgary, the province's two largest cities.It is one of Canadian Army's busiest military training bases and its airfield is also used by the Royal Canadian Air Force. It population fluctuates but more than 1,000 people can be based there at any given time.

schema.headline: Canadian military base fire: Death toll confirmed and cause under investigation

title: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate
description: Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across FranceFigure caption, Watch: James Waterhouse speaks to looted shop owners on the streets of Pari
body: Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across FranceFigure caption, Watch: James Waterhouse speaks to looted shop owners on the streets of ParisByJack BurgessUpdated 1 hour agoFrench President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday.In a national address from the Élysée Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame."Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted". Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry.The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice.Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Local officials said the Limoges town hall was "largely lost" after fire caused part of the building to collapseOn Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon.Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police. Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history.In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold.Image source, Mairie de LimogeImage caption, A view of the damage inside Limoges town hall on Sunday morningSpeaking near the ruined building, Annèyse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody.""It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before."Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Fires were lit and shops looted during smaller scale disorder in Paris on SundayWidespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings.The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations.Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places.France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.Image source, ReutersImage caption, A man tries to extinguish a fire in Paris on SundayStudent protests which began last month escalated significant on Saturday after they were joined by trade union members and other anti-government groups.The response from political figures has pointed to France's deep political divisions as the country prepares for an election in April which could see the hard-right pitted against the hard-left.France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.Jean-Luc Mélenchon - leader of the hard-left La France Insoumise party - heavily criticised Nuñez and police chiefs on social media. He said they had "shown complete incompetence" with their handling of the demonstrations and called them "specialists in organised chaos".Meanwhile, the leader of the hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the "exploitation" of anger "by political forces that encourage violence".

schema.headline: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate

title: Man, 80, who died in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond named
description: Image source, FacebookImage caption, Ian Haggis - pictured when he was younger - died when the light aircraft crashed near Loch LomondByClaire Diamond
body: Image source, FacebookImage caption, Ian Haggis - pictured when he was younger - died when the light aircraft crashed near Loch LomondByClaire DiamondBBC ScotlandUpdated 5 hours agoAn 80-year-old man who died in a light aircraft crash is understood to be flying instructor Ian Haggis. He and a 16-year-old boy died when their plane came down near Loch Lomond. The teenager's identity has not been released. The pair had flown out from Glasgow Airport at 16:17 and stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of the village of Drymen near Stirling.Emergency services were called to the crash at about 16:45 on Friday.Both of them were pronounced dead at the scene. Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) carries out its inquiries.Old Drymen Road, near the scene of the crash, remains closed with vehicles being turned around and hillwalkers rerouted.Tributes posted on social media by former students describe the flying instructor as "a gentleman and an experienced aviator", and a "good friend". The plane - a Piper Tomahawk II aircraft - is registered to Leading Edge Flight Training in Renfrew, according to the Civil Aviation Authority's aircraft register., external Previous social media posts on Leading Edge's Facebook page report the instructor's nickname as the 'Flying Haggis', and show that he had been working with the flying school. A spokesperson for Leading Edge Flight Training said: "We are devastated by this tragic accident involving one of our aircraft and two close members of our Leading Edge family."Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with the families, friends and loved ones of those who lost their lives."Leading Edge Flight Training is assisting with the investigation and while it remains ongoing we are unable to say anything further at this time."Image caption, Stuart Abernethy saw the crash from his garden Stuart Abernethy told BBC Scotland News that he witnessed the last few moments of the plane's journey from his driveway."I was standing in the drive and I heard an aircraft engine over-revving," he said."I looked up... and I saw probably for about the last 10 seconds a light aircraft coming down in a spiral. I didn't see it land and I didn't hear anything - but I just saw it vanish from sight."There was no smoke, no impact sound or anything like that. And then nothing."He added: "It was low and it wasn't in a sort of dive trajectory, it just literally fell out of the sky in a spiral with the engine revving and then a total silence after that."Normally we hear training flights and hear them recover and minutes later they appear and you're relieved. But there was just deathly silence after that."Later, his daughter saw the news about the crash on social media."It was very unpleasant to see, it's scary to see actually - and then when you learn that some people had lost their lives, it's a very distressing experience."Image caption, Police remained at the scene on Sunday and blocked off Old Drymen Road near the crash Gavin Birch-Williams, managing director of Glasgow Airport, said: "We are aware of an incident involving a light aircraft that departed from Glasgow Airport."This is a deeply tragic event, and the thoughts and heartfelt sympathies from all at Glasgow Airport are with the friends and families affected."The plane had earlier taken off from Cumbernauld Airport at 11:46, before flying 15 minutes to Glasgow Airport.It stayed there until about 13:00, before doing a two-hour flight north east to Newport-on-Tay then turning round and heading back to Glasgow.It was on the ground at the airport for just over an hour before it took off again and started its final flight.

schema.headline: Man, 80, who died in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond named

title: Suspects hunted after police officer injured in shooting in Nottingham city centre
description: Neghat Khan, leader of Nottingham City Council, said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" by news of the shooting. "My thoughts and full support are
body: Neghat Khan, leader of Nottingham City Council, said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" by news of the shooting. "My thoughts and full support are with the injured police officer, their family, and their colleagues across Nottinghamshire Police," she added.​"Nottingham City Council is working tirelessly alongside the police to support the investigation and ensure those responsible are swiftly caught and brought to justice.​"While incidents of this nature are extremely rare, our commitment to keeping Nottingham safe is absolute. "Thanks to the daily bravery of our police and community protection officers, Nottingham remains a safe city, and residents can be assured that every available resource is being deployed."In a post on social media, Nadia Whittome, MP for Nottingham East, encouraged anyone with information to contact the police. "My thoughts are with the injured police officer and his family following this truly shocking incident," she wrote. "We all wish him a full and speedy recovery."

schema.headline: Suspects hunted after police officer injured in shooting in Nottingham city centre

title: Search for Amelia Earhart's plane resumes after stormy weather
description: Image source, Purdue UniversityImage caption, Sirisha Bandla (right), pictured with expedition lead Steve Schultz, said the crew was "really excited"B
body: Image source, Purdue UniversityImage caption, Sirisha Bandla (right), pictured with expedition lead Steve Schultz, said the crew was "really excited"ByAleks PhillipsA search for the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote island in the Pacific Ocean has resumed after severe weather caused researchers to stop for several days.A team has travelled to Nikumaroro Island, part of Kiribati, hoping to solve the mystery of the famed aviator's disappearance by investigating the so-called Taraia Object, spotted in the atoll's lagoon in aerial imagery.The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation about her fate.Rough seas and strong winds forced the team to remain on their research vessel for three days, until the weather cleared on Sunday."We are finally getting off the ship and able to land on Nikumaroro," Sirisha Bandla, a technology specialist who is part of the expedition, said in a video update from the deck of the Marin Mainiku.The researchers arrived at the uninhabited atoll last week and began an underwater survey of the area of interest. But the weather - powered by strong El Niño conditions in the Pacific - has so far prevented them from beginning a second of three phases, in which underwater objects will be probed to determine their depth and sediment will be dredged.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937"We're working to get everything done today if we can," Bandla said. "The crew's really excited."Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937.From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California.But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel.One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.Images of the so-called Taraia Object - which Purdue University says is visible in photography dating back to 1938 - show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters, though other explorers remain sceptical.Image source, Archaeological Legacy InstituteImage caption, A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object in a lagoon on NikumaroroInterest in the expedition prompted New Zealand's Air Force Museum to publish, external previously unseen reconnaissance images of Nikumaroro on Friday.While the Taraia Object is not obviously visible in any of the black-and-white slides, taken in 1938 from a seaplane, they do show the beached wreck of the SS Norwich City, a British merchant vessel that ran aground on the island during a storm in 1929, killing 11.Purdue, which with the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) is spearheading the expedition, said the incident demonstrated the risks surrounding the island.To get into the atoll's lagoon, a boat has to navigate through a narrow gap created in the reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited.But the university said wind gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph) present around the island until Sunday meant the transport boat could be knocked into the reef by crashing waves.Image source, RNZAFImage caption, Images from 1938 released by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand this week show Nikumaroro - then Gardner Island - with the SS Norwich City wreck in the bottom right cornerHowever, it said the Norwich City wreck may lend credence to the researchers' theory. Purdue said a 15-year-old in Florida reported hearing Earhart's voice repeating "New York City" over her father's shortwave radio shortly after the aviator vanished. Proponents of the castaway theory argue this may have been a misunderstanding of Earhart giving her location as near the Norwich City.As a result of the three-day hold, the research team has extended the expedition time to complete its fieldwork and has yet to indicate whether they had found any promising evidence of Earhart's plane.ALI director Rick Pettigrew said the team was aware of the global interest in the expedition and would share its results "as soon as we are able". Purdue suggested before the poor weather hit that it could identify the Taraia Object in a matter of days.While researchers have previously found evidence of a human presence on the island around the time of Earhart's disappearance, some skeptics believe the Taraia Object was just a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the lagoon.Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short.In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation.Similarly, an expedition in 2019 to investigate a photograph of what might have been landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.

schema.headline: Search for Amelia Earhart's plane resumes after stormy weather

title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
description: Figure caption, The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raidBy Quentin SommervilleInternational
body: Figure caption, The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raidBy Quentin SommervilleInternational correspondent, Columbus, OhioWarning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicideThe few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood."This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars."You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune.We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape. Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.America's War on Drugs: The Synthetic WaveExtraordinary access shows how strong synthetic drugs are changing America's drug crisis.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," says Mike as he lights up a few grains of fentanylImage source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Mike, a former army veteran, acts as our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States.At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over.It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl.The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added.When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce."Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me.They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat.Recovery group offering hopeAt the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma.They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty.One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life.As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid."It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting at Glenwood ChurchImage source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, One of those gathered at the church, Tonya, recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same timeBoth in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose"."In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers.Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so."The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it."Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Scott Sanders, 65, is almost 10 years sober and runs Hope DealersOverdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds.His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina.That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine."The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements."And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois.Watch the documentary on YouTube, externalI meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity.Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means.He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever.When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico. "If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability."And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear.  "Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me.A novel approach Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening."In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart, who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel."The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures.Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens.It was indeed, as Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters."Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained.Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, In Chicago's largest jail, drugs were soaked in the pages of books and in lettersIn August, I joined Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search.As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of.As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates.The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells, where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper.Now every piece of post that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters that enter the jail test positive for moistureOutside the jail's walls, it's not hard to encounter the effects of the synthetic drugs wave on Chicago's streets. In the west of the city, day and night, men and women are bent double, swaying, as Mike did, as fentanyl and other synthetics surge through them.In the upscale Oak Park neighbourhood, the local metro station has a vending machine that dispenses naloxone for free. Nearby, a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair has deep wounds in his legs, likely from xylazine use. He's being tended to by 40-year-old Karen Bell.Karen is a recovery worker with the group Liv4Lali. A former heroin user, she's 17 years free from hard drugs.She exudes kindness, and when I ask her about the drugs being used now, she says, "so many things are being mixed in right now. And it's affecting our bodies, whether it's the wounds, whether it's the withdrawals - and sometimes wounds can extend to the point where it's life changing."Her organisation, like Hope Dealers in Columbus, distributes test strips which check drugs for fentanyl, medetomidine, xylazine and other adulterants.The drugs now, says Karen, are "way more dangerous"."Because before, back in my day, I stopped using heroin 17 years ago, right. That was still heroin. When you bought that you knew it was heroin. But now, when you buy a bag, you don't know really what it is," she tells me.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Karen, a recovery worker, tends to a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair in an upscale part of town Dart has been sheriff of Cook County for 20 years, so I ask him how the war on drugs was progressing. "I don't think there's anybody involved with it who would sit there and say it's a raging success. It's not," he tells me. And the new problem, he says, reiterating the Chicago drug dealer, is synthetics."The tradition has always been that law enforcement had an even more vital role because everything that was potent was coming across the border, whether it was coming from Colombia, Mexico, China, the poppy fields of Afghanistan. Now, with the explosion of synthetic drugs, people can do this in their house, in their sink, in their bathtub, you name it."Victory in the war on drugs won't come from focusing just on the supply side, the sheriff adds. "Front and centre there's got to be huge substance abuse treatment," he says, mentioning a number of recovery programmes running in his jail. "You can reduce the market if you can address people's issues with substance abuse. And I know many people who, after long struggles, have come out on the other side in a really good way."'A lot of people are struggling'Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby, now 17. After our meeting at the metro station, I meet them both in a country park in a suburb outside Chicago. With typical care, Karen tells me to watch out for the poison ivy as we walk along a muddy track.It wasn't far from here, around 17 years ago, that she was at her lowest ebb.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Karen says her pregnancy was an opportunity to get clean. She's 17 years free from hard drugs As the wind blows through a tall oak tree beside us, she says: "The day I found out I was pregnant, I was on my way to commit suicide. I was so fed up with trying to quit. I was so fed up with living in a tent in the woods, using a bucket. I was so fed up with losing my friends and family because I was just so ashamed."A pregnancy test changed her mind. She then spent time in Cook County jail for theft. Her parents, sensing an opportunity for her to get clean, refused to pay her bail money. So Karen got clean and Abby was born inside the jail.When I ask Abby, who wants to become a tattoo artist, whether she's ever been tempted to experiment with drugs, she says: "Nah, I've seen it mess with my family too much, with my dad, my mum, killing my aunt, my uncles. You know, it's not worth it to get high for like a couple of hours."She continues: "There's a lot of people are struggling, especially that our country is raising our prices, raising the prices on food and it's causing it. A lot of mental health now is very expensive so people can't get help, and one way they can turn to that is by drugs."Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis, but it is never the same crisis. It has shifted from heroin, to prescription opioids to fentanyl and now to a whole new range of synthetics.Successive administrations have fought - and lost - the war against drugs. The dealers, the suppliers, the cartels and users all adapt, always a few steps ahead of efforts to stop them.Additional reporting by Darren ConwayIf you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

schema.headline: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis

title: Pierre Sage apologises to Crystal Palace fans after the Eagles are thrashed by Brighton
description: Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage said he felt "shame" at the Eagles' performance during their 5-0 thrashing by Brighton and did not know whether he
body: Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage said he felt "shame" at the Eagles' performance during their 5-0 thrashing by Brighton and did not know whether he would be given time to save his job.Sage's side conceded three times in the opening 10 minutes as they suffered their worst loss to their rivals since January 1956."It's my fault because I am the coach, I gave the motivation. I prepare the situations. We played so bad it's my fault," said Frenchman Sage, who was only appointed Palace manager in the summer."It's difficult to summarise because there are a lot of negative points."We started really bad. It's completely not normal to concede three goals in this kind of game after nine minutes."I prepare the team, that is why I am responsible of what's happened on the pitch. I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing."Asked if he will get time to turn Palace's poor form around, he said: "I don't know."Under his predecessor Oliver Glasner, Palace enjoyed the most successful phase in the club's history, lifting the FA Cup for the first time in 2025 and then winning the Conference League in May. But Sage has had a tough start at Selhurst Park since he arrived after guiding Lens to the French Cup and second in Ligue 1 last season.Palace are 14th in the Premier League with two wins from seven games but their 17 goals conceded are the most in the top flight."I just want to apologise to the fans," added Sage.  "We were not at the level we expected, and I'm really sorry for that because I know how important it is for them, but we didn't show today that it's really important for us too."Asked on his emotions after the game, he replied: "Only one feeling - shame. When you play this kind of game you have to show another face. It was our worst face."Palace, with one win and one loss from their two Europa League matches, play on Thursday with a trip to Turkey to take on Besiktas before returning to Premier League action on Sunday at home to Newcastle.

schema.headline: Pierre Sage apologises to Crystal Palace fans after the Eagles are thrashed by Brighton

title: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says Health Secretary Yvette Cooper
description: The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.Yvette Cooper told the BBC the
body: The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.Yvette Cooper told the BBC there would be new standards for caring for children in A&E in England, with figures collected on corridor care by age for the first time.She was speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg where the programme highlighted the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.The health secretary has announced £140m to improve urgent care in England ahead of what she said would be a "more difficult" winter than usual.The government has already pledged to end corridor care for all patients by the end of this parliament, and now Cooper has said eradicating it for children would be prioritised. Corridor care refers to patients receiving treatment or waiting in corridors, waiting rooms or other hospital areas due to a lack of appropriate space.The health secretary was also asked if the government would meet a key manifesto pledge that 92% of patients would start treatment within 18 weeks of booking a hospital appointment by 2029. "That remains our manifesto commitment and of course we're going to keep working towards it," Cooper said.Pushed further on whether the target was achievable, she replied: "The whole point about having the targets is about having something stretching that we work towards." The 18-week target has consistently not been met for more than a decade. Cooper said that the NHS was dealing with a number of challenges after record A&E admissions following heatwaves over the summer.According to the latest figures for England, an estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients. On the programme the story of Finlay Roberts, was highlighted. He died after being discharged from hospital in 2024 following hours spent in an A&E corridor in north London.Finlay's father David told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor. "He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to her son in the corridor.Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor." The Whittington Health NHS Trust where this happened extended their condolences to the family.They said they continued to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and at times some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors. "Our staff work tirelessly to provide safe and compassionate care in extremely challenging conditions," they said.On Friday health groups - including Age UK, Marie Curie and the Royal College of Nursing (RCN), also expressed their concern over corridor care, writing a letter to the health secretary urging her to take action.It said the practice was fundamentally incompatible with NHS care standards and it would require "whole-system action" to eradicate it.This weekend Cooper announced £140m funding to boost urgent care capacity as part of an effort to deal with the impact of seasonal illnesses, including flu and norovirus.The money will go towards 14 schemes across England, including new urgent care centres, ambulance fleets and upgrades to emergency departments.Shadow health secretary Damian Hinds said the government needed to act, but asked it to explain where the money was coming from.It comes after almost 7.3 million people attended A&E between June and August in England, according to NHS data, the highest ever figure for a summer period.Health thinktank the King's Fund warned that the service was facing a "twin crisis" going into the winter, with little time between peak periods for staff and the system to recover.NHS leaders are urging eligible people to get flu vaccinations, with medical director Prof Frankie Swords saying earlier this month there were "ominous" signs of winter pressure already affecting hospitals.Swords said there were more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year. RCN England's executive director Patricia Marquis said the extra money was welcome but would ultimately provide "just another sticking plaster on a system that is at breaking point"."The nursing workforce needed to deliver these services goes into winter already running on empty and short of staff," she said.Correction 18 October 2026: This article and this note have been updated after earlier versions incorrectly stated the location of Finlay Roberts' death.

schema.headline: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says Health Secretary Yvette Cooper
